p: Kew Palace has a poignant chapter in its story. George III spent time here during his periods of illness, and Queen Charlotte died at Kew in 1818, which is why the palace feels frozen in that moment. Elsewhere in the gardens, Queen Charlotte's Cottage, a rustic retreat used by the royal family for picnics, is another lovely link to the same era.

Once you've explored the palace, Kew Gardens has plenty to fill the rest of the day. The Palm House, the great Victorian glasshouse full of tropical plants, is a must, and the Temperate House is even bigger. Up in the trees, the Treetop Walkway gives you a bird's-eye view of the woodland canopy. Kids love the Hive, a huge, buzzing sculpture inspired by bee life.

Getting here is easy on public transport. Kew Gardens station is served by the District line and the London Overground, and it's a short walk to the Victoria Gate entrance. Wear comfy shoes, as the gardens are big and you'll easily walk a few miles without noticing.
Combine it all with a riverside walk along the Thames, and you've got a full, peaceful day away from the busy centre of London. Pack a picnic if the weather's kind, as the lawns are made for it.
